strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: cross-referencing majority-voted pseudo-labels between original and rephrased questions is a simple, principled way to mitigate the collapse problem of single-view self-reward RL, and the paper articulates the intuition (contrastive agreement as implicit induction) reasonably well.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: six base models across two LLM families, seven benchmarks spanning math, code, instruction-following, and multi-task knowledge, plus test-time training experiments, ablations on the rephrased data, voting-accuracy analyses by difficulty level, and qualitative case studies showing reward hacking in baselines.

Consistent empirical gains over strong self-reward baselines (Self-Certainty, Entropy, Majority-Voting) with training curves that visibly avoid the collapse behavior exhibited by baselines, and results competitive with or exceeding GT-reward in several settings (e.g., +6.8% on MATH500 for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct).
Good reproducibility practices: implementation details, hyperparameters, prompts for question rephrasing, evaluation libraries, and publicly released code.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a combination of known components — question paraphrase augmentation, majority-voting pseudo-labels (TTRL/SRT-style), and GRPO. The 'contrastive agreement' framing is largely narrative; there is no theoretical analysis of when cross-referenced agreement converges to correct labels or why it resists collapse.

Dependency on an external strong model (Qwen3-32B) to generate rephrased questions weakens the 'self-supervised without external supervision' positioning; rephrasing cost and quality are not ablated (e.g., number/quality of paraphrases, rewriter scale, noisier paraphrases).

Modest and somewhat mixed gains: improvements over the strongest baseline (Majority-Voting) are often within ~1-2 points, LiveCode results are inconsistent (Co-Reward trails 'Majority-Voting w/ Rephrased' in the ablation), and the headline 'surpasses GT reward' claim rests on one model/benchmark combination while GT-reward wins on several other cells; no variance estimates or multiple seeds are reported.

Training is confined to the MATH training split, so claims of general elicitation of reasoning ability across domains (code, instruction following) are indirect; the collapse-mitigation mechanism is not disentangled from simply training on more (duplicated) data — a baseline of majority-voting on the union of original+rephrased questions without cross-reference would strengthen the analysis.

The framing spends considerable space on conceptual motivation while the algorithmic contribution (Eq. 6-8) reduces to a two-term GRPO objective with swapped pseudo-labels; the acknowledged residual risk of reward hacking on complex questions is left unresolved.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: reward hacking / training collapse in self-reward RL for LLM reasoning, and the cross-referencing of pseudo-labels between a question and its paraphrase is a simple, sensible mechanism to combat single-view consistency bias.

The empirical evaluation is broad: six base LLMs across two families, seven benchmarks spanning math, code, instruction following, and multi-task, plus test-time training experiments and several ablations (rephrased-data impact, voting accuracy over training steps and difficulty levels, qualitative case study).

The analysis of voting accuracy during training (Figures 4-5, Appendix D.2) provides useful mechanistic insight into why majority-voting collapses on hard problems and how cross-referencing mitigates it.
The paper is generally well written and reproducible in spirit: implementation details, hyperparameters, evaluation libraries, and the rewriting prompt are all provided.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core method reduces to self-training with majority-vote pseudo-labels on data-augmented (paraphrased) inputs, i.e., cross-view consistency, which is a well-established idea in semi-supervised learning and self-improvement (e.g., self-consistency, STaR-style bootstrapping, augmentation-based self-training). The 'contrastive agreement' framing oversells what is essentially an augmentation-consistency regularizer on top of GRPO with majority voting.

The 'fully self-supervised / no external feedback' claim is undermined by the reliance on Qwen3-32B as an external rewriting model. This introduces a stronger external model into the pipeline, and there is no analysis of paraphrase errors (cases where the rewrite changes the math semantics or answer), which would directly corrupt pseudo-labels. The compute cost of rewriting and double rollouts is acknowledged but no compute-matched comparison is given (e.g., majority-voting with 2x rollouts or on more data).

Gains over the majority-voting baseline are modest and inconsistent: Co-Reward underperforms Majority-Voting on LiveCodeBench in several settings and on parts of IFEval, and the reported average gains of ~2% over the closest baseline are within plausible seed variance. No error bars, variance over seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported.

Training and evaluation are heavily math-centric: RL is performed only on the MATH training split, so claims about general 'reasoning' elicitation and cross-domain transfer (code, instruction following) rest on indirect evidence from relatively small deltas.

The 'reaches or even surpasses ground-truth reward' claim needs more careful qualification: GT reward itself collapses in their setting, and the comparison is only against a single GT-reward configuration; the theoretical motivation (Section 3.2) remains conjectural with no formal analysis of when contrastive agreement is a valid reward proxy.

Missing ablations that would test the central hypothesis: sensitivity to the number/quality of paraphrases, behavior when the rewriter is weaker or the same policy model, and comparison against other anti-collapse mechanisms (e.g., KL tightening, early stopping, reward normalization).

strengths: The core idea is intuitive and well-motivated: cross-referencing majority-vote pseudo-labels between a question and its paraphrase makes reward hacking harder than single-view self-consistency, and the paper provides a clear dual-path formulation (Eqs. 6-8) and a simple, reproducible algorithm.

Empirically thorough: six base models across two families (Qwen2.5/Qwen3, Llama-3.2), seven diverse benchmarks (math, code, instruction following, MMLU-Pro), test-time training experiments (Table 2), ablations on rephrased data (Table 3), training-dynamics analyses of voting accuracy by difficulty level (Figs. 4-5, 7), and qualitative case studies.

The collapse analysis is a genuinely useful empirical contribution: the voting-accuracy curves showing Majority-Voting degrading on hard problems (Levels 4-5) while Co-Reward remains stable directly support the central claim about mitigating collapse.

Reproducibility is reasonable: implementation details, hyperparameters, the exact rephrasing prompt, and public code are provided, and the extra IFEval metrics and full generation transcripts are given in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The method is essentially input paraphrase augmentation combined with majority-vote pseudo-labeling (self-consistency, Wang et al. 2022; STaR-style self-training) inside GRPO. Eq. 6 is just the sum of two GRPO objectives with swapped pseudo-labels; there is no new theoretical insight or analysis of when cross-referenced pseudo-labels are provably better (e.g., error correlation between the two views is never quantified).

Insufficient differentiation from and comparison against the closest prior work. The related work cites SRT (Zhao et al., 2025a, 'Consistent paths lead to truth'), Co-rewarding (Zuo et al., 2025), INTUITOR, RENT, etc., but the experimental comparison is restricted to Entropy, Self-Certainty, and Majority-Voting. Given how close SRT and Co-rewarding are in spirit, omitting head-to-head comparisons is a significant evaluation gap.

The 'label-free / self-supervised' claim is weakened by the pipeline: rewrites are generated by an external, stronger model (Qwen3-32B), so the method is not truly self-contained, and the correctness of rewrites is never verified — a flawed rewrite silently injects wrong pseudo-labels into both views. No measurement of rewrite quality or failure rate is reported.

Rigor of the headline claims is questionable. Results appear to be single runs with no variance/significance reporting, and several gains over baselines are 1-2 points. The claim that Co-Reward 'surpasses GT reward' (e.g., +6.8% on Llama-3.2-3B) is surprising and under-analyzed — the paper does not explain why pseudo-labels from majority voting would outperform true labels, which deserves deeper investigation rather than being presented as a selling point.

Scope is narrow: training uses only the MATH training split; all other benchmarks are transfer evaluations. The framework's behavior on code/logic-domain training data is untested, and the added computational overhead (double rollouts for both views) is acknowledged but not quantified against compute-matched baselines.

Writing and polish issues: repeated grammatical errors ('without without reliance', 'consistently generate wrong output'), a miscited reference (Hendrycks & Dietterich 2019 corruption benchmark used for input-variant motivation), and the naming is confusingly close to the existing 'Co-rewarding' method, which should be explicitly disambiguated.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: training collapse and reward hacking in label-free/self-rewarding RL for LLM reasoning, and the diagnosis (single-view supervision creating a 'self-consistent illusion') is clearly articulated.

The proposed framework is conceptually clean: two orthogonal instantiations (data-side analogy-invariance via cross-referenced paraphrased questions, and model-side temporal invariance via an EMA-updated teacher) both reduce entanglement between the reward signal and the online policy.

Empirical evaluation is broad and thorough: multiple model families (Qwen2.5/2.5, Qwen3, Llama3) and scales, three training sets (MATH, DAPO-14k, OpenRS), seven diverse benchmarks (math, code, instruction-following, multi-task), plus test-time training experiments.

The analysis sections are convincing: validation curves showing baselines collapse while Co-rewarding remains stable, reward/response-length curves distinguishing genuine improvement from reward hacking, and pseudo-label accuracy analysis supporting the necessity of the EMA teacher.
Ablations (Table 3) properly isolate each component, e.g., removing EMA updates or replacing cross-supervision with single-view majority voting, and results support the design choices.
Reproducibility is reasonably good: implementation details, hyperparameters (Table 5), the exact rephrasing prompt, evaluation libraries, and a public code link are provided.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the individual components: Co-rewarding-II is essentially a Mean Teacher / BYOL-style EMA self-distillation applied to GRPO pseudo-label rewards, and Co-rewarding-I is majority-voting pseudo-labeling (à la TTRL/SRT) applied across paraphrased views. The contribution is a combination and adaptation of well-known techniques rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the theoretical justification for why temporal/data invariance prevents collapse is only intuitive, not formal.

Co-rewarding-I relies on Qwen3-32B to generate rephrasings, which weakens the 'fully self-supervised/label-free' claim and introduces an external dependency; the paper acknowledges the method still collapses on DAPO-14k, indicating data-dependent stability.

Statistical rigor is lacking: results appear to be single runs with no variance, confidence intervals, or seed reporting. Several benchmarks are small (AMC has 83 questions), so reported gains (e.g., +2-5%) may not be statistically significant.

Headline claims of surpassing GT-Reward are selectively favorable: in several settings (e.g., Qwen3-4B-Base on DAPO-14k, where Co-rewarding-I trails Entropy on GSM8K; OpenRS LiveCode where Co-rewarding-I drops to 28.91 vs GT 39.00), the method underperforms baselines, and these inconsistencies are not deeply analyzed.

The compute overhead of double rollouts (policy + teacher rollouts in Co-rewarding-II, original + rephrased rollouts in Co-rewarding-I) is not quantified or compared against baselines in a compute-matched analysis, which matters for a fair efficiency assessment.

Writing and presentation have noticeable issues: inconsistent terminology ('initiations' vs 'instantiations'), typos ('stepbystep', 'argentic', 'traind', 'Pseuo'), and an empty code URL in the abstract.

Potential long-term collapse of Co-rewarding-II is not ruled out: the EMA teacher ultimately learns from the student's pseudo-labels, and experiments run only 300-330 steps; the stability claim would be stronger with longer-horizon evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: training collapse and reward hacking in label-free/self-rewarding RL for LLM reasoning.

The unifying 'cross-view invariance' framing drawn from self-supervised learning (SimCLR/BYOL-style views) provides a coherent conceptual lens that connects Co-rewarding-I (data-side) and Co-rewarding-II (model-side).

Comprehensive empirical coverage: multiple model families (Qwen2.5/Qwen3/Llama), multiple scales, three training sets, diverse evaluation benchmarks (math, code, instruction-following, MMLU-Pro), plus test-time-training experiments.

Useful diagnostic analyses: reward/length curves distinguishing reward hacking from genuine improvement, pseudo-label accuracy tracking (Figure 6), and an honest report that Co-rewarding-I itself still collapses on DAPO-14k.
Ablations (original-only vs. rephrased-only supervision, removal of EMA updates) are informative, and the rephrasing prompt and training details are released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Co-rewarding-I is essentially majority-voting pseudo-labels (TTRL/SRT-style) applied to a paraphrased twin of each question, and Co-rewarding-II is a mean-teacher/EMA self-distillation scheme directly transplanted from BYOL/DINO/Co-teaching. The contribution is combination and application rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the theoretical grounding for why cross-view supervision prevents collapse is only intuitive, not formal.

The 'label-free' claim is overstated: Co-rewarding-I depends on an external Qwen3-32B model to generate rephrased questions, introducing a significant hidden cost and a form of external knowledge that baselines do not use. This weakens the comparison against label-free baselines and the practical scaling story.

Results are inconsistent across settings, undercutting the headline claims. Co-rewarding-I collapses on DAPO-14k despite the paper's stability framing, and in several tables (e.g., Table 2 Qwen3-4B GSM8K: 75.89 vs. 90.07 for Majority-Voting; Table 7 Qwen2.5-7B) the method underperforms existing baselines. The +3.31% average gain is modest and not supported by statistical significance testing, multiple seeds, or variance reporting.

The 'surpasses ground-truth RLVR' claim needs more careful analysis. The comparison appears to compare different effective training lengths/configurations (Table 5 shows different train steps and KL coefficients for I vs. II), and self-supervised pseudo-label training on GSM8K-style problems plausibly acts as a strong regularizer relative to noisy GT rewards; without controlled analysis this claim is more intriguing than supported.

The reward design may implicitly encode correctness rather than escape it: agreement between a question and its paraphrase is a proxy for answer stability, which can still be hacked by consistent-but-wrong answers on both views; the paper acknowledges rephrasing-quality dependence but does not analyze failure modes (e.g., cases where both views yield the same incorrect majority answer).

Several experimental details reduce comparability and confidence: no seed/variance reporting, different training-step budgets across methods, all baselines reimplemented in-house without reproducing published numbers, and evaluation temperature (0.8) differing from training temperature (1.0) without justification.

Significance is somewhat narrow: gains concentrate on GSM8K (a benchmark near saturation for these models) while AMC/LiveCode gains over the best baselines are marginal or negative, limiting the evidence that Co-rewarding elicits genuinely harder reasoning rather than stabilizing easy-question training.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: training collapse/reward hacking in label-free, self-rewarding RL for LLM reasoning, and frames it clearly through the lens of self-supervised learning (invariance across views).

Proposes two complementary instantiations (data-side contrastive agreement via rephrased questions; model-side EMA teacher distillation), and the framework is well-motivated and cleanly presented with formal objectives and pseudo-code.

Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple model families and scales (Qwen2.5/3, Llama), three training sets, seven evaluation benchmarks spanning math, code, instruction-following, and multi-task ability, plus test-time training experiments.

Strong analysis beyond headline numbers: training/validation curves showing baselines collapse while the proposed method remains stable, reward and response-length dynamics, pseudo-label accuracy tracking, ablations of each component (original vs. rephrased-only training, EMA removal), difficulty-level voting analysis, and qualitative case studies of reward hacking.
Good reproducibility signals: implementation details, hyperparameter tables, evaluation library details, and publicly released code.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Co-rewarding-I is essentially majority-voting (TTRL-style) pseudo-labeling applied across paraphrased question pairs, and Co-rewarding-II is a mean-teacher/EMA self-distillation scheme transplanted from BYOL/DINO-style SSL; both ingredients are well established, and the contribution is mainly their combination and empirical packaging rather than a new algorithmic mechanism.

The 'label-free' claim deserves more scrutiny. Co-rewarding-I depends on an external, much larger model (Qwen3-32B) for question rephrasing, and the paper does not ablate sensitivity to the rephrasing model's quality or quantify rephrased-question correctness (a rephrasing error silently injects wrong pseudo-labels).

The central stability claim only partially holds: Co-rewarding-I still collapses on DAPO-14k, meaning one of the two proposed variants fails on one of the three training sets; the paper offers only a plausible post-hoc explanation about data 'background richness' rather than a predictive account or principled fix.

Claims of surpassing ground-truth RLVR (e.g., 94.01% Pass@1 on GSM8K vs. GT) are surprising and under-explained. Possible confounds (pseudo-label noise acting as regularization, effective training-set differences, evaluation variance) are not analyzed, which weakens the strength of this headline claim.

No statistical rigor: results appear to be single runs with no variance/seeds or significance testing, yet many reported deltas between methods are small (often <1–2 points) and could be within noise.

Baseline coverage is narrow (three self-rewarding baselines); several closely related recent label-free/self-play methods mentioned in the related work (e.g., SRT, SERL, TTRL variants) are not empirically compared, making the SoTA claim harder to verify.

No theoretical or formal analysis of why cross-view supervision prevents the self-consistent illusion; the argument remains intuitive, and the abstract's quantitative claims are slightly inconsistent with the body (+3.31% vs. +3.46%).

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent terminology ('initiations'/'instantiations'), typos ('stepbystep', 'traind'), and the compute cost of the extra teacher/reference rollouts in Co-rewarding-II is not quantified relative to baselines.
